question: As part of Valencia’s year as European Green Capital – awarded to it by the Commission for 2024 – a conference was organised on ‘Conservation and management of wetlands to tackle climate change’.

José Gosálbez, a representative of Valencia City Council and a member of Devesa-Albufera Municipal Council, publicly declared to all those attending the conference that the problem with the Albufera wetland ‘is not climate change, climate alarmism or climate religion’ and that ‘all this talk of a climate bubble has merely been an ideological decoy and a waste of public money’.

He also said at the event – organised under the auspices of the Commission – that ‘many scientists, including Nobel prize winners, have already distanced themselves’ from the definition of climate change1. In view of these statements by a public representative at a European Green Capital event, promoted by the Commission: 1.
Does the Commission believe that there is scientific evidence on climate change and the corresponding global warming?
In its view, what scientific evidence is there regarding the impact of global warming on European wetlands such as the Albufera wetlands?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.4.2024) There is scientific consensus on climate change: that the earth is warming, and that this is due to greenhouse gas emissions, produced by human activities. EU climate action is based on science, including the goal to reach climate neutrality by 2050 and strengthen societal preparedness and resilience to the negative impacts of climate change.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) sixth Assessment Report (2023)1, representing the unchallenged state of scientific findings, is unequivocal in saying that: ‘Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming’.
Also, the IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land2 concludes that wetlands are high-carbon ecosystems affected by different pressures, including human-induced climate change.

Protecting existing carbon stocks prevents the release of greenhouse gas into the atmosphere and, in the case of wetlands, is also beneficial for increasing ecosystems’ resilience while improving biodiversity, water security and human well-being. In this vein, the Wetlands Conference was organised to raise awareness about these linkages.
